transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-03
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Brooks (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (OakBridge Head of ML), Priya Rao (OakBridge Infra), Daniel Kim (OakBridge CTO)

Auto Summary: Quick Optimize walkthrough focused on real-world batching/prefetch savings for session-heavy financial chat application. Discussed hit-rates, TTLs, prefix-length heuristics, concurrency limits, and Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs for compliance. Agreed on pilot and info exchange.

Topics covered: batching windows, prefix/KV prefetch, sessionization, cost-simulator, security (KMS/VPC/SOC2)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Ethan: hey everyone thanks for joining, I see we have Liam, Priya, Daniel, and my teammate Maya. quick agenda: we want to run through the Optimize playbook — batching + prefetch (prefix/KV) and how that maps to your cost profile and latency SLOs, then decide pilot scope. sound good?
[00:14] Liam: yep sounds good. quick context: we run a financial assistant inside the OakBridge web console, ~peak 600 qps but heavy day/night skew, many sessions with repeated user context — about 70% of requests are short clarifying queries.
[00:28] Priya: and from infra side we have regulatory routing concerns, we might need KMS in a specific region and prefer VPC connectivity. also curious if Dedicated is required or Hosted with VPC will be sufficient.
[00:42] Maya: got it. we'll map workload to two high-leverage levers: batching/concurrency and prefix/KV prefetch. the idea: batching reduces per-token cost but can add latency tail; prefetch (we often call it "prefix cache" or KV prefetch) amortizes static context tokens across requests.
[00:58] Daniel: can you show the numbers — like how batching + prefetch combo affects cost per 1k requests?
[01:10] Ethan: yes we'll walk the cost-sim. quick note — some transcripts list the product as "Optimize Console" or "Optimize toolkit" — we're calling the module Optimize here.
[01:22] Maya: okay I'll share my screen on the cost-simulator. (screen noise) there's a toy workload already loaded — I used a 30-token avg prompt and 120-token avg response, with a sessionized prefix of ~80 tokens repeated across 60% of requests.
[01:40] Maya: baseline: no batching, no prefix cache -> raw hosted per-token rate X. with batching window of 50 ms and concurrency cap of 32, batching saves ~18% tokens per second because CPU/GPU pipeline is more filled.
[02:00] Liam: wait is that 50 ms window real? our UX needs <200 ms p95 for immediate replies.
[02:08] Maya: yes the window here is small; the tradeoff is the first token latency can see ~+10-30ms but p95 depends more on queueing during peaks. we can target strict latency budgets by combining small batching windows + session-affinity routing to keep hot sessions on warm KV-local nodes.
[02:26] Priya: session affinity — can you expand? we currently have sticky sessions on our side but not for model inference.
[02:34] Maya: session-affinity means routing a given user session to the same VM/pod that holds the KV cache and warm KV cache for their prefix; this gives much higher prefetch hit rate and lower latency since we avoid remote fetch. it increases routing complexity but yields 30-60% improvement in tail latency for session-heavy workloads in our tests.
[02:58] Daniel: what about cache TTL and invalidation? our prefix includes recent transactions that must expire quickly.
[03:06] Ethan: good point. two patterns: 1) prefix cache with short TTL (e.g., 5m) for transactional tokens; 2) persistent prefix for stable context (user profile) with longer TTL. we recommend per-key TTLs; Redwood's KV supports TTLs and invalidation hooks in Dedicated and Private deployments.
[03:28] Liam: are there gotchas with hit-rate assumptions? we have many one-off queries too.
[03:34] Maya: yes you should provide a request distribution — we asked for a 7-day histogram — because hit-rate sensitivity is non-linear. to illustrate, I vary the prefetch hit rate here from 20% up to 80% and you can see cost savings curve flattens after 65% because batching benefits saturate.
[03:56] Maya: also prefix length matters — shorter prefixes (20-40 tokens) have higher reuse but less absolute token savings; big prefixes (100+ tokens) save more per hit but require more memory and slightly longer prefetch time.
[04:14] Ethan: I want to flag the difference between 'K-V cache' and 'prefix cache' language — product docs sometimes say KV but ops teams think key-value store with different SLA. they are the same capability in our runtime: it's an LRU-backed KV with optional prefetch pipeline.
[04:30] Priya: ok. security — does prefetch store PII? we can't keep raw transactions in cache without encryption.
[04:36] Maya: Redwood supports customer-managed KMS for both Dedicated and Private deployments, and disk+transfer encryption. for Hosted we have envelope encryption but if you need HSM-backed keys we recommend Dedicated or Private.
[04:54] Daniel: that's leaning us towards Dedicated then. the cost delta — how big is it?
[05:00] Ethan: it depends on commit size and utilization. Dedicated gives better unit cost under high sustained throughput and gives you data isolation and KMS control. for short pilots Hosted with VPC + KMS envelope might be fine if you can accept the smaller compliance gap. we'll send a clear pricing comparison in the follow-up.
[05:20] Liam: can we dig into concurrency more? our peak spikes to 600 qps — what happens to batching then?
[05:28] Maya: two regimes: at very high QPS batching windows can be smaller because natural concurrency fills the batch; at low QPS you need longer windows to hit good packing. the cost-simulator has a "traffic shape" slider — you can upload your histogram and it simulates effective batch sizes and expected latency.
[05:48] Maya: (shares link) I'm toggling from peaky to steady traffic. notice when we add prefix prefetch with a 60% hit-rate the effective token count drops and average GPU utilization increases, which lowers effective per-token cost by ~22% in this scenario.
[06:10] Priya: any locks or shared state when using prefetch? we need to avoid thundering herd if invalidation floods.
[06:18] Maya: we've built anti-thundering features: jittered refresh, request coalescing, and a fallback to model-local generation if KV fetches miss. also our runtime can do staggered pre-warming to avoid spikes.
[06:34] Ethan: quick clarification — Redwood's Optimize Console will recommend batching window and concurrency caps automatically based on your request histogram; you can override them if you have stricter latency targets.
[06:48] Liam: how do you measure ROI? is it tokens-per-second saved, or dollars saved per 100k requests?
[06:56] Maya: both. value is usually dollars per 100k requests (we compute host unit cost + tokens saved). in the spreadsheet I'll annotate the formula: effective_unit_cost = base_model_unit * (1 - savings_from_batch_and_prefetch) + infra amortization for Dedicated.
[07:14] Daniel: what about model routing/fallbacks? if the preferred model is offline, do you fallback to a smaller quantized model?
[07:22] Maya: yes, the runtime supports model variants and quantized fallbacks. Optimize suggests which model variants to route to based on cost/latency policy. can do canary rollouts too.
[07:34] Priya: on the pilot scope — what do you need from us to run a realistic simulation?
[07:40] Ethan: three things: 1) 7-day request distribution with timestamps (even aggregated buckets ok), 2) token histogram (prompt/response median and p95), 3) example prefix templates (what tokens go into session prefix).
[07:54] Liam: we can extract that from our analytics — I think we can share aggregated histograms without PII.
[07:58] Priya: on network, we need an architecture diagram for VPC peering and expected outbound IPs for compliance.
[08:06] Maya: we'll attach our VPC peering guide and a short diagram. for Dedicated we can ship an on-prem package if you prefer airgap but that requires longer lead time.
[08:20] Ethan: demo time — Maya, can you step through a simulated run with our sample traffic?
[08:26] Maya: yep. pulling up the sim — baseline run (no prefetch, batching 0ms) shows average latency 120ms, p95 340ms, cost $Y per 100k. now enable prefix prefetch with 50% hit-rate and batching window 25 ms. average latency goes to 110ms, p95 280ms, cost down ~16%.
[08:48] Liam: interesting — p95 improved as well. I thought batching hurts tail.
[08:52] Maya: it can, but prefetch reduces work per request so it reduces queueing too. also small batching windows reduce the added latency but still capture some packing wins.
[09:04] Daniel: are these numbers from Hosted or Dedicated profile?
[09:08] Maya: Hosted profile; Dedicated usually shows a lower per-token base cost but you add reserved infra amortization in. I'll add both columns in the spreadsheet.
[09:20] Priya: can the Optimize Console export suggested configs to Terraform or k8s manifests? we prefer infra-as-code.
[09:28] Maya: yes there's an export option: a config bundle that includes batching/concurrency and KV TTLs that you can apply to Dedicated or Private clusters. Hosted gets the same params via API.
[09:36] Liam: let's talk about unusual traffic — sometimes we have sudden large prompt inputs (like whole policy docs).
[09:42] Maya: for large prompts we recommend offloading to background async paths or chunking. prefetch helps less for one-off huge prompts. Optimize can flag long-tail token loads and suggest throttles or async routing.
[09:56] Ethan: security Q: SOC2 / ISO?
[09:58] Daniel: yes and we need to track audit logs per request for regulatory review.
[10:04] Maya: Redwood provides request-level audit logs, retention configs, and you can ship logs to a customer S3 with KMS envelope. SOC2 Type II attestation is available and we'll attach the certs.
[10:16] Priya: on the KMS note — we need HSM-backed keys in EU region. is that supported?
[10:22] Ethan: for Dedicated and Private yes, for Hosted we support customer-managed keys but not direct HSM in all regions — we'll confirm region availability in the follow-up.
[10:34] Liam: one more question about prefetch accuracy — if we prefetch based on predicted next tokens will that ever degrade quality?
[10:42] Maya: prefetch only caches KV attention states for known prefixes; it doesn't change model weights. false positives are just cache misses with a small extra fetch. we also have a conservative prefetch heuristic tuned for high precision and lower recall to avoid polluting cache with noisy prefixes.
[10:58] Ethan: ok time check — about halfway. anything critical to add?
[11:04] Liam: can you show the sensitivity chart for hit-rate vs savings again?
[11:08] Maya: sure toggling. (screen) here's the curve: at 25% hit -> 7% cost savings; 50% hit -> 18% savings; 75% hit -> 27% savings. it's workload-dependent but demonstrates non-linear returns.
[11:28] Daniel: and memory footprint for 75% hit on 600 qps?
[11:32] Maya: about 120 GB of KV across the cluster in this model, distributed LRU. this is why Dedicated hardware with more RAM per GPU can be beneficial.
[11:44] Priya: how do we monitor hit-rate in production?
[11:48] Maya: Optimize console has per-route cache metrics: hit/miss rate, average KV latency, prefetch queue depth, and token-saved counters. we can alert when hit-rate drops below threshold for a route.
[12:02] Ethan: question from Redwood side — do you have retention rules for session data?
[12:06] Liam: regulatory requires rolling 30 day retention for audit but we prefer not to store sensitive tx data in cache beyond 5 minutes.
[12:14] Maya: we can set short TTL for transaction keys and longer for profile keys. we'll document recommended TTLs and how to use tags to classify keys.
[12:26] Daniel: pricing ask — can you show Dedicated committed discount examples?
[12:30] Ethan: yes in the follow-up sheet we'll show tiered committed monthly throughput and effective per-token price net of commit.
[12:40] Priya: regarding deployment timeline — how long to stand up Dedicated environment?
[12:44] Maya: typical provisioning timeline is 4-6 weeks after contract; Private on-prem longer. Hosted pilot can start in 1-2 weeks depending on integration.
[12:56] Liam: pilot success criteria — what do you recommend?
[13:00] Maya: 4 success criteria: 1) cost delta >= 15% vs baseline OR consistent p95 improvement while maintaining cost neutrality, 2) stable hit-rate > 50% for prefetched keys, 3) latency SLO met (client p95 < 200 ms), 4) security checklist satisfied (KMS/VPC/SOC2 items).
[13:18] Ethan: let's capture that as the acceptance criteria for the POC.
[13:22] Daniel: agreed. what's the smallest scope we can run to validate?
[13:26] Maya: replicate top 3 intents across 2-week traffic window — that usually surfaces the hit rate and concurrency shape.
[13:34] Priya: ok. on compliance doc sharing — we'll want the data processing addendum and support for subprocessor list.
[13:42] Ethan: we'll attach the DPA and subprocessors list in the follow-up.
[13:46] Maya: quick demo item — exporting a suggested config. I'm exporting a config bundle now — it includes batching 25ms, concurrency cap 48, per-route TTLs and prefetch policy. file name: oakbridge-config-20261103.zip (link).
[14:02] Liam: nice. can this be previewed before apply?
[14:06] Maya: yes the console shows a dry-run with expected metrics.
[14:12] Daniel: switching topics — how do we handle sudden model updates that might regresses output quality?
[14:18] Maya: Optimize ties to our eval hooks — you can bind prompt sets and have regression alerts. if quality drops, routing can fallback to a previous model and flag the rollout.
[14:28] Priya: any concerns about increased operational complexity for our platform team?
[14:34] Ethan: there is modest added ops work for Dedicated (maintain nodes, monitor KV), but we provide CI templates, dashboards, and a runbook. for Hosted we manage most of it.
[14:44] Liam: last technical — co-located KV caches: do you ever replicate hot keys across nodes?
[14:50] Maya: yes we support selective replication for very hot prefixes to reduce cross-node fetch. that's configurable per-route.
[14:58] Ethan: ok time to wrap — recap of next steps and owners.
[15:04] Maya: I'll produce the annotated cost-simulator runs (Hosted vs Dedicated), share the config bundle, and run the pilot once we get OakBridge sample traffic.
[15:12] Liam: we'll extract the histograms and share them privately.
[15:16] Priya: I'll loop in our security/compliance lead and share network requirements.
[15:20] Daniel: sounds good. thanks folks.
[15:24] Ethan: thanks all — follow-up email with attachments and a proposed pilot schedule for next week.
